## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — This Isn't About Picking a Repository
We won't be creating a Zenodo account or clicking through a real deposit
form today. The specific repository you'll eventually use depends on your
field, your funder, and your data — that's a decision for later, with
your librarian. What matters today is the *shape* of what every deposit
process asks for, so none of it is a surprise when you actually need it.
:::

## Packaging Your Project for Someone Else

Every arc so far has quietly been building toward this moment. The
README you were asked to write in Arc 1, the file naming conventions
from Arc 2, the `.gitignore` and commit history from Arc 6 — all of it
is exactly what a real data or code repository asks you to produce at
deposit time. There's no new skill left to learn here. There's just a
new name for what you've already been doing: **packaging**.

### Writing a README That Could Survive Being Downloaded by a Stranger

A repository deposit lives or dies on its README. Open your project's
`README.md` — the one you started in Arc 1 — and check it against what
an actual deposit would require:

```markdown
# Project Title

## Description
One paragraph: what is this project, and what question does it answer?

## Data
Where the raw data came from (source, URL or accession number, date
accessed), and what license or use agreement governs it.

## Files
A short list of what's in each folder and what it contains —
`raw_data/`, `processed_data/`, `scripts/`, `outputs/`.

## How to Reproduce This
The exact steps someone else would run, in order, to get from
`raw_data/` to your result. If you've been using `renv`, say so, and
say which R version you used.

## Citation
How you'd like this project cited, if someone reuses it.

## Contact
Who to contact with questions, and how.
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Why "A Stranger" Is the Right Standard
The test for a good README isn't "would I understand this?" — you
already do, you wrote it. The test is "would someone who has never seen
this project, and can't ask me anything, get it running?" That stranger
is usually future-you, eighteen months from now, having forgotten all of
it.
:::

### Documenting Your Environment, Automatically

A README can describe your setup in prose. R can also just *tell you*
exactly what it was, with no risk of the description drifting out of
sync with reality:

```{webr-r}
sessionInfo()
```

This single function call — R version, operating system, every loaded
package and its exact version — is the kind of thing a real data
package often asks you to include directly, sometimes as its own file
(`sessionInfo.txt` or similar). It's `renv`'s snapshot, read back to you
in plain language.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-tip"></span> Learn More — Where This Actually Goes
When you're ready to deposit for real, a few common destinations:

- **[Zenodo](https://zenodo.org)** — general-purpose, issues a DOI,
  widely accepted by funders and journals
- **[OSF](https://osf.io)** — project-level, good for packaging code,
  data, and materials together as one unit
- **[Figshare](https://figshare.com)** — similar to Zenodo, popular in
  some fields over others

Most funders and many journals now also require a **data availability
statement** in the manuscript itself — a sentence or two saying where
the underlying data lives and how to access it. If your field has a
standard, field-specific repository instead (a gene expression database
for genomics, for instance), that often takes priority over a
general-purpose one. Your library's research data services can help you
figure out which applies to you.
:::

### What a DOI Actually Buys You

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — Citable, Not Just Downloadable
A repository deposit usually earns a **DOI** — a permanent link that
won't break even if the file moves, gets renamed, or the hosting service
redesigns its site. That permanence is what lets someone else *cite*
your data the same way they'd cite a paper — and what lets you point to
a fixed, unchanging version of your work, instead of "whatever's
currently in my Google Drive folder."
:::

## The Limits of Reproducibility

Back in Arc 2, before any of this started, we put up a list:

> **R's Flexibility Creates New Responsibilities**
>
> - **Efficiency** — You can still write code that runs slowly
> - **Best practices** — R is agnostic to readability, optimal analysis,
>   data ethics
> - **Data management** — Explicit instructions are needed to select
>   and organize pipelines, folders, files
> - **Information** — Code that runs is not always code that produces
>   desired or understandable results

Seven arcs later, you can read every line of that list and recognize
exactly which habit answers it — `renv` and functions for efficiency,
`here()` and naming conventions for data management, error messages and
testing for information. Reproducibility, as this course has taught it,
is the answer to **"can this be run again, by someone else, and get the
same result?"**

That's a real, necessary thing. It's also not the whole question.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-warning"></span> Watch Out — Reproducible Isn't the Same as Right
A perfectly reproducible pipeline — pinned packages, committed history,
documented every step — can still analyze the wrong population, apply
the wrong definition, or answer a question nobody should have asked in
the first place, with full fidelity, every single time it's run. Running
the same flawed analysis twice and getting the same flawed answer twice
is not a correction. It's just a well-documented mistake.
:::

### A Live Example of This Exact Trap

ARCS's companion extension, *Analyzing Research Data with Claude Code*,
walks through a real version of this. Students there ask an AI coding
agent to estimate a published health statistic, and compare what happens
when a single hidden decision changes — not a bug, just a quiet choice
about how to handle a missing survey answer. The script still runs
without error. It's still fully reproducible — anyone re-running it gets
the identical number back. But depending on that one choice, the result
ranges from roughly 48% to over 90%, for the same underlying data.
Nothing in that pipeline *looks* broken. The code runs is not always code
that produces desired or understandable results — Arc 2's warning,
wearing new clothes.

That extension calls this the **garden of forking paths**: when it's
cheap to try "just one more" version of a definition or a filter, and
you report the version you like best, reproducibility doesn't save you.
It just means your selectively-chosen answer is now permanently,
verifiably reproducible — which is a strange kind of trust to have
earned.

### Who the Data Is About, and Who Decides

Two frameworks, often mentioned together, ask a question reproducibility
never does:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## <span class="dot dot-note"></span> About This — FAIR and CARE Principles
**FAIR** — Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable — describes how
research outputs should be structured so others (including future-you)
can find and use them. Everything in the packaging section above is, in
effect, FAIR in practice.

**CARE** — Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility,
Ethics — centers who the data is *about*, particularly for Indigenous
data governance, asking not just "can this be reused" but "should it be,
and by whose permission."

FAIR asks whether data *can* be found and reused. CARE asks whether it
*should* be — and who gets to answer that. A dataset can score perfectly
on every FAIR criterion and still have been collected, shared, or reused
in a way the people it describes never consented to.
:::

### Meet R Where It's At — One More Time

Arc 2 closed its own list with a set of habits, not warnings:

> R Projects · README · File Naming Conventions · Workflow automation ·
> Look beyond R

Every one of those became a full arc. That's the shape this entire
course has had: name a responsibility that comes with power, then build
the specific habit that answers it. Data ethics doesn't get a habit in
the same way — there's no function call, no package, no checklist item
that resolves "should this be reproduced at all?" That question doesn't
go away because you've finished a course. It's meant to stay open.

::: {.instructor-note}
**<span class="dot dot-important"></span> Instructor Note**

Let the discussion questions below actually sit — don't rush to supply
an answer, and don't let students treat this as a problem with a correct
solution to find. The goal is the opposite of every prior arc: this is
the one place in the course where "I'm not sure" is the honest and
correct response. If the room goes quiet, that's the material working,
not a sign to fill the silence.
:::

**For discussion:**

- Think of a dataset or analysis you're familiar with. Who was it *about*?
  Were they consulted about how it would be used?
- Is there a difference between data you have *permission* to use and
  data you have *standing* to use?
- Arc 7 showed that AI-assisted code can run perfectly and still be
  wrong. Is a dataset with no FAIR/CARE consideration behind it a
  version of the same problem — technically functional, substantively
  compromised?

## What We Did, and Why

**What we built, across all eight arcs:** a reproducible project, start
to finish — a managed environment (`renv`), organized files and a
README, vectors and functions, dynamic Quarto reports, tidyverse
cleaning pipelines, a committed git history published to GitHub, a
checklist for auditing AI-generated code, and — today — a package ready
to hand to someone else, with an honest accounting of what packaging
can't settle on its own.

**Why it matters:** Arc 2 opened this course with a warning: R's
flexibility creates new responsibilities, and nothing about the language
enforces good habits for you. Everything since has been one answer after
another to that warning — a specific habit for each specific risk.
Today's isn't a habit. It's the reminder that the habits have a edge.
Computational reproducibility is necessary for trustworthy science. It
has never been sufficient. A perfectly reproducible pipeline can still
answer the wrong question, on the wrong data, without the right
permission to ask it in the first place — and no package, pin, or commit
history will tell you that on its own. That part stays on you.
